rules.statement: simulate, explain and analyze call the same Engine.evaluate as enforcement, and explanations are built by the enforcing flow. simulate, explain and a shadow window's comparison decide on the documents enforcement reads, by its one rule (ViewDocuments): the platform's, the tenant's, and the app's when the scope has roles in that app or the tenant document decided with (the head, the candidate, or the revision explained) binds one of that app's permission policies to Anyone or a principal; never more. What explain reports as the revisions decided on, and the documents simulate takes a candidate of, are those the view read: a tenant document that does not compile makes a roleless request read no app document. A shadow window's candidate is decided with the failures of the documents it reads, and only those: a tenant candidate that no longer reads an app document is not indeterminate for that document's failure, and one that starts reading an app document that cannot be read or does not compile is (#1410). A candidate of a document that does not compile replaces that failure with itself; one of a document the view could not read is not compared (BASE_MISMATCH). A simulated or explained request that sends a header the documents of its view read with different values is refused 400, as enforcement refuses it before evaluation (PIP-12). An http resource goes through the path normalization every request's path does (PathNormalizer; RC1-41): a path enforcement answers 400 (a dot segment after one decoding, an empty segment, an encoded separator or a backslash (PIP-14), a malformed escape, over 2,048 characters as written or 256 per segment once decoded (PIP-5)) is refused 400, by the one function enforcement's checks use (PathNormalizer.enforceable), and the normalized path, its path parameters removed, is decided; a typed resource is held to the same length bounds, as written. analyze takes its resource the same way. analyze resolves a binding's policy as the engine does: a built-in control-plane policy from the engine's own statements (BuiltinPolicies.CONTROL), never counted opaque (#1401); a break-glass binding of cosec:root is listed as an allow marked break-glass, conditional on its window, with that window. An http action goes through the reading every request's method does (PIP-18), by the same function: a verb with a lower-case letter is refused 400, and http:HEAD is decided, and analyzed, as http:GET.

A publish goes on only while its change holds the slot, checked again right before its head write; the change that took a slot and finds the head its holder wrote over the same base records why it failed. Any other change waits (409).

rules.statement: The history of a document is the chain of its head. rules.statement: A control-plane change records how its author was identified, and each change event how the operator of its step was (`origin`): `asserted` is true when the host believed the identity the caller stated (the `CoSec-Identity` header, `STA-9`) instead of verifying a credential itself; `via` is the credential as stated or verified (its method, its id, never its value, and the request's id); `peer` is the address of the connection the request arrived on, read from the Reactor Netty channel beneath any forwarded-header handling (`server.forward-headers-strategy`, a `ForwardedHeaderTransformer`), so that a caller cannot state it as it states its client address; a host that cannot read it that way, any but Reactor Netty, records none. It is read where the control routes are served, never on the request path of the others. A step no request drives, a maintenance pass for one, records none. The member is additive: a stored change without it reads, and a reader that does not know it ignores it. An event written as JSON carries the member only when it has one.

rules.source: RFC 0007 §10.2 (maintainer decision 2026-11-21, the control-plane host's service API; control-server-design §0.7, §0.8)
rules.statement: The control API's service profile is the narrow set a service that calls the control plane directly may ask for, served on a port of its own (`cosec.control.http.service-port`, WebFlux only; the network, not a filter, says who may use it): the tenant and app documents (their reads, and `:apply` on a tenant's) and the change flow that needs no person, of a tenant's or an app's document (propose and check, read, list, rebase, abandon, run or skip the shadow window, publish); a change made through it is always analyzed as the principal it states, with the roles it states: no one is the trust root through the service profile (CTL-81), so a change publishes alone only what the analysis proves that principal holds (and a holder's roles-only change, by the role class, CTL-79), and anything else waits for a person, who approves on the operators' port. A workload the network admits to the port can therefore publish alone what any principal and roles it states hold, in any tenant. Every other route is a `404` before the control plane is asked, as if it did not exist: the platform document, approvals and rejections, rollback, break-glass, the queries and propagation. Nothing but the control API is served on that port. The profile narrows what is served and never widens what the caller may do: each route it serves is authorized for the stated principal by the policies. The service port is not the application's or the management port, and it is refused with the control API off (`cosec.control.http.enabled=false`, which serves no control route at all) or beside the gateway's statement (`only-gateway-can-reach`), since a service port admits services. The listener stops by unbinding, waiting for the requests in flight within the shutdown grace, and closing every connection still open, the idle keep-alive ones included.

rules.statement: Within one control-plane instance, a change listener receives the events of one change in the order the instance wrote them: one queue and one consumer per listener, and those who wait for room in a queue are served in the order they came, so a smaller event never queues ahead of a larger one put before it. A gated step waits for its REQUIRED listeners to record its event after what was queued before it, within the required timeout, or fails (503); a REQUIRED listener's full queue, or its call that fails or does not answer, loses, counted and logged at ERROR, the event of a step already stored, never failing it; a BEST_EFFORT listener's full queue drops the incoming event, so what arrives is an ordered prefix. The queues hold together at most a thirty-second of the heap; a listener that stops answering is reported, never cut off. At shutdown the listeners stop taking events and deliver what is queued within the drain timeout; what is left is counted and logged (ERROR for a REQUIRED listener) before they stop, and a gated step arriving meanwhile is refused (503). Across instances, a consumer orders by each event's time and the change's record.

rules.source: RFC 0007 §7.4.7 (control-typed-api decisions of 2026-11-21: writer model B, the role class cosec:manage-roles)
rules.statement: The role class: a change of a tenant's document that only writes or removes roles (putRole, removeRole), by an author who holds cosec:manage-roles on that document, needs no second person on account of who grants, unless one of those roles has no app or is of the control plane's own app (cosec.control.app-id), the role written or the one the head holds under its id, which a putRole replaces and so removes: putting or removing such a role is analyzed as before and waits for a person, since a member of it holds control calls on its tenant's document, governors of the control plane being for a person to appoint. The exclusion is keyed on the role's app, not on its actions' names, and that is enough: a binding a tenant's role derives is scoped to its app, and a control request is decided in the control app, so a role of any other app permits no control call whatever its catalog's actions say. It sees every escalation of the change, the grant analysis's and the others' (a break-glass binding's), and lifts only when every one is one it may lift, each safe for a holder: CROSS_TENANT is a service principal's case, a principal outside the tenant projecting its roles; NOT_COVERED arises for a holder inside the tenant handing out catalog permissions it does not itself hold, which is what managing roles means; DENY_OVERLAP arises when a DENY that binds the author may overlap what the role grants, and a DENY still binds whomever it binds at decision time (deny-first), so lifting the overlap grants nothing a DENY forbids. It records one informational ROLE_CLASS escalation in their place, naming the holder and what it lifted; anything the analysis could not tell (an unreadable app document, an unresolved policy, a spent budget) still waits. cosec:write on each role and cosec:grant on each binding a role derives are decided as before; a change that writes anything else is analyzed whole; an app's or the platform's document is never the class's. The grant is decided again at publish, as the publisher, on the current heads, as the whole grant analysis is: a grant withdrawn after the check, while the change is checked, shadowing or ready, sends it back to AWAITING_APPROVAL, and nothing publishes. A check answers the same: a holder learns the change will not wait, anyone else the escalation it would wait on. Its bounds are the format's: a tenant's document holds no "*" role and the platform's none at all; a tenant's role derives only bindings of its own tenant's members, in its app, to the permission policies that app's document defines (a tenant cannot write a perm: policy, and a permission its app does not define does not publish); a member reaches nothing outside its own tenant's document, whatever the app's catalog grants (TenantIsolation); the tenant's boundary caps what such a role permits.

No other status carries the member, and no 409 is answered without it; `detail` still explains the case to a person and is no contract. No conflict but SLOT_HELD carries `heldBy` (`contract/control/conflict.json`). The typed write call (`proposeAndPublishWithoutShadow`) abandons the holder only when it is a change of the same author left CHECKED, SHADOWING or READY and not updated for at least the write's patience, by the control plane's times (the holder's updatedAt against the createdAt of the change the write just proposed): a writer that died holds the document for one patience. rules.statement: A control request has no deadline of its own: the deadline is its caller's, and it reaches the request by cancellation. In process (LocalControlService) the caller's coroutine runs the request. Over the network, HttpControlService aborts its exchange when its caller is cancelled or its call times out (cancel(true): the JDK client closes an HTTP/1.1 connection, resets an HTTP/2 stream), and the WebFlux control routes, which the service port serves, run the request in a coroutine of the response's subscription, which the server cancels when the connection ends. On a Servlet host the operators' port runs the request to its end on its thread: a servlet container does not tell a handler that its client went away, so a request there ends within its bounded waits, as one cancelled after its head write does. A publish cancelled before its head write publishes nothing and leaves its change as it stood, READY and holding its own slot: a slot belongs to a change, never to a request. What it wrote before the cancellation is left as a failed publish leaves it (RFC 0007 §5.4): a PUBLISHING record with no outcome, a pending entry or record that reclamation removes as an orphan (CTL-72). Publishing the change again publishes it. From the head write on (the write, settling the change, releasing its slot, recording its outcome and what moved meanwhile) it does not respond to cancellation and runs to its end; one that fails there is settled by publishing again, adding no revision (CTL-2). A stage cancelled while it writes its candidate gives its slot back. Every wait of a control request is bounded on its own, those that do not respond to cancellation included, so none outlives its caller by more than its bound: the pipeline's decision by cosec.pipeline.timeout; the forced read of the documents the control checker confirms by the snapshot store read timeout (30 s); a REQUIRED change listener by cosec.pipeline.timeout; the detection of moved heads by its own timeout (1 s); every compare-and-set loop by its attempts (16; 4 authorization batches); each command of the Redis control store by CoCache's command timeout (cocache.redis.command-timeout, 2 s by default), a disconnected client refusing at once. No wait is on another request's release: a held slot is a 409, a held lease is a skipped pass, and an in-process lock is held for one bounded read at most. So no property sets a control request's deadline: what can be computed is not configured, and only the caller knows how long it will wait.
